Convolutional Networks: Learning to See Leaf Disease

Step 1: one filter by hand · Step 2: train a small CNN on bean leaves · Step 3: look inside the network
In Part 1 we saw that a neural network learns its own features: its hidden layers re-draw the data so that the classes become easy to separate. Images need a special kind of layer to do this well: the convolutional layer. In this notebook we will:
  1. Apply one filter by hand to a bean-leaf photo, to see what a convolution does.
  2. Train a small CNN to recognize two bean diseases and healthy leaves.
  3. Look inside the trained network to see the filters it learned on its own.

Step 1: One filter by hand

A small filter (kernel) slides over the image and lights up where its pattern appears.
A convolution slides a small grid of numbers, the kernel (or filter), across the image. At each position it multiplies the kernel with the pixels underneath and adds them up. A large result means "the pattern this kernel looks for is here". The output image is called a feature map. Two ideas make this efficient:
  • Local receptive field: each output value only looks at a small 3×3 patch, not the whole image.
  • Weight sharing: the same 9 numbers are reused at every position of the image.
Pick a kernel and a leaf below. The stride is how many pixels the kernel jumps each step: a larger stride gives a smaller feature map.

Step 2: Train a small CNN on bean leaves

Field photos of bean leaves in three classes: angular leaf spot, bean rust and healthy.
The beans dataset (Makerere AI Lab, Uganda) has photos of bean leaves taken in the field with a phone. It is the same dataset as Session 1, here reduced to 128×128 pixels so it trains quickly. The data comes already split into a training set (to learn from), a validation set (to watch progress during training) and a test set (the final exam).
Training: 1034 images    Validation: 133    Test: 128

Two more building blocks: ReLU and pooling

After each convolution, ReLU keeps only the positive responses, and max pooling shrinks the feature map by keeping the strongest response in each small block.
ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) is a very simple rule applied to every number in the feature map: negative values become 0, positive values stay as they are.
  • It turns each feature map into a clean answer to "is my pattern here, and how strongly?" Negative responses (for example, an edge going the opposite way) are simply ignored.
  • It is the activation function that makes the network non-linear. Without it, stacking many layers would be no more powerful than a single layer. The MLP in Part 1 used the same ReLU.
Max pooling splits the feature map into small blocks (here 2×2) and keeps only the largest value of each block: 
1 3 | 0 2
5 2 | 1 1          5  2
----+----    →
0 4 | 8 6          4  8
1 2 | 3 7
  • Width and height are halved, so there are 4× fewer numbers to process.
  • If a spot moves by a pixel, the result barely changes: what matters is whether the pattern is present, not its exact position.
  • After pooling, the next layer's 5×5 filter covers a larger region of the leaf.
Using the Vertical edge kernel on the bean rust leaf from Step 1.

The architecture

Our CNN stacks three blocks of convolution → ReLU → max pooling, followed by a small fully connected layer that makes the decision.
Flattening a 128×128 color image gives 49,152 numbers. A single fully connected layer with 1,000 neurons would need about 49 million weights, and it would treat neighboring pixels as unrelated. The CNN re-uses each small filter everywhere, so it needs only a tiny fraction of that (compare the totals in the table below).

Training

Train Model trains the network live; Load Pre-trained loads the same network trained longer beforehand.
Train Model trains a new network from random weights on the chosen number of training images (about 30 seconds with the default settings). Because we only train for a few epochs live, the result is modest. Load Pre-trained loads the same network that was trained beforehand for 40 epochs on all training images, with flipped and rotated copies of the leaves to make it more robust.

Results for the pre-trained network (40 epochs, all training images)

Test accuracy: 80%

Chance level (guessing): 33%
Each row is the true class, each column the network's answer. Numbers on the diagonal are correct; the others show which diseases get confused.

• The loss measures how wrong the network is; it should go down as training proceeds.
  • The validation curve uses images the network does not learn from. If training accuracy keeps rising while validation accuracy stalls or drops, the network is overfitting: memorizing the training images instead of learning the disease patterns (as in Part 1).
  • The test accuracy is measured only once, at the end, on images never used for any decision.

Step 3: Look inside the network

The filters the network learned in its first layer, starting from random numbers.
Nobody programmed these filters: they started as random numbers and were adjusted during training. Each tile is one 5×5 color filter. Compare them with the hand-made kernels from Step 1: many become edge detectors or color detectors (for example, brown-yellow spots vs. green leaf).

One test leaf passed through the network: bright = where a filter responds.
Each image below is a feature map: the output of one filter (after ReLU) for the chosen leaf. Bright areas are where that filter's pattern was found. We show the 6 filters of layer 1 and layer 2 that are most active on average over all training images. The same filters, in the same order and with the same brightness scale, are shown for every leaf, so you can compare how each filter reacts to healthy and diseased leaves. Layer 2 maps are half the size because of max pooling. The network's answer for this leaf is shown underneath.

Layer 1 responds to simple things such as edges and colors. Layer 2 combines them into textures, such as the rust-colored spots, and because of pooling it looks at a larger region of the leaf. Much deeper networks continue this hierarchy up to whole objects. This is the same idea as in Part 1: the network learns its own features, now organized in space.

How much of the leaf does one neuron see?

Each neuron looks at a small patch of the layer below, but stacking layers makes that patch grow: deeper layers see a larger part of the leaf.
The region of the input image that one neuron depends on is its receptive field (or support. Left, without pooling: every layer uses a 3×3 kernel. One neuron in layer 2 looks at a 3×3 patch of layer 1, and each of those 9 neurons looks at its own 3×3 patch of the image. Together they cover a 5×5 patch of the input. Every extra 3×3 layer adds only 2 more pixels. Right, with pooling (our network): after a 2×2 max pooling, each step of the next filter moves 2 pixels in the original image, so the field grows much faster. Our network uses a 5×5 filter, pooling, a 5×5 filter, pooling, then a 3×3 filter: one neuron of its three conv layers sees 5×5, 14×14 and 24×24 pixels. That is enough for a rust spot but not the whole leaf. Much deeper networks stack enough layers to see the entire image.

data.text/markdown:
What to notice

  • A convolution is a small filter sliding over the image; it lights up where its pattern appears.
  • A CNN learns its own filters from labeled examples, and stacked layers build edges → textures → shapes.
  • CNNs use far fewer weights than a fully connected network on images, but they still need many labeled examples to work well.

Questions for discussion

  1. These photos were taken in the field in Uganda. Would the model work on bean or coffee leaves photographed in Amazonas? What could go wrong with a model trained only on lab photos?
  2. What would a useful filter look for in a microscopy image of spores or nematodes?
